title: The computational Kesten–Stigum threshold for sparse community recovery
formal: Do there exist a fixed integer q≥5, fixed rational constants a>b>0 satisfying (a−b)²<q(a+(q−1)b), a constant δ>0, and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm A such that, for every sufficiently large n, A weakly recovers the communities of the symmetric stochastic block model SBM(n,q,a,b), with expected overlap at least 1/q+δ?
definitions: Generate the hidden labels σ₁,…,σₙ independently and uniformly from [q]={1,…,q}. Conditional on these labels, each unordered pair of distinct vertices is independently an edge with probability a/n if its labels agree and b/n otherwise. Thus the graph is simple and undirected; take n≥a. Equal prior probabilities make communities asymptotically balanced, but their sizes are not conditioned to equal n/q. The algorithm receives this one graph and knows q,a,b; it receives no planted labels or auxiliary samples. It outputs a label vector σ̂∈[q]ⁿ. Define overlap(σ̂,σ)=max over permutations π of [q] of n⁻¹Σᵢ 1{σ̂ᵢ=π(σᵢ)}. The expectation in the question is over labels, graph edges and the algorithm’s random bits. Weak recovery means a fixed positive advantage over the limiting chance baseline 1/q. Running time is worst-case polynomial in n on a standard bit model, for every graph and random tape; the algorithm and polynomial exponent may depend on the fixed parameters but not on n. Put d=(a+(q−1)b)/q and θ=(a−b)/(a+(q−1)b). The strict inequality is dθ²<1, below the Kesten–Stigum threshold. All three model parameters remain constant as n grows.
answer_criterion: A positive answer must exhibit one fixed parameter choice below the threshold and prove the stated polynomial running time and nonvanishing expected overlap for all sufficiently large n. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm at every fixed parameter choice in the formulation. Recovery with unlimited computation does not answer the question. An algorithm with q growing with n, a result only above the threshold, or a lower bound conditional on an unproved computational hypothesis is partial progress. The question does not impose an extra promise of information-theoretic recoverability: any positive algorithmic example automatically has that property.
context:
Community detection asks whether the edges of a network reveal an underlying partition. Here every vertex has the same expected degree, regardless of its group. Consequently, sorting vertices by degree cannot directly identify their communities. The signal is in the pattern of connections between vertices, and each vertex has only a constant expected number of observations even as the network grows.

The target is deliberately much weaker than recovering every label. A constant-degree graph has many isolated vertices, whose memberships cannot be inferred from their incident edges. Weak recovery asks only for a fixed improvement over random guessing on average. Permuting all community names must be allowed: renaming the hidden groups changes neither the graph distribution nor the quality of an inferred partition.

The quantity dθ² compares the growth in the number of observed neighbours with the decay of label information along an edge. In a local tree approximation, d describes branching and θ describes how much a child’s label remembers its parent’s label. This explains why the value one is a natural boundary for algorithms based on propagation of small correlations. It does not by itself prove an impossibility result for algorithms that use the whole graph.

Abbe and Sandon prove efficient recovery above this boundary for every fixed number of communities. Their method uses an acyclic form of belief propagation and addresses the effect of cycles in the finite graph. This supplies the algorithmic side of the proposed threshold. The question asks whether a qualitatively different method can succeed strictly below it in the assortative case a>b.

There really are parameters for which the graph contains useful information below the Kesten–Stigum threshold. Banks, Moore, Neeman and Netrapalli establish such regimes for at least eleven groups in the assortative model. Their recovery argument permits exponential computation, searching over sufficiently plausible partitions. Their five-group statement concerns the disassortative case, where between-group edges are more likely; that is a different parameter range from this card.

This produces a concrete computational-versus-statistical puzzle. The missing labels are not intrinsically unidentifiable everywhere below the boundary, yet known efficient methods do not recover them throughout the information-theoretically possible region. An affirmative answer to this card would refute the universal fixed-community barrier with a single parameter example. A negative answer would establish that the obstruction is computational wherever recovery is statistically possible.

Ding, Hua, Slot and Steurer give conditional evidence in 2025. In their parameterized symmetric model, a low-degree conjecture implies a strong computational lower bound for recovery below the threshold by a fixed margin. Their recovery definition uses correlation with the centred membership matrix. The result is a reduction from a conjecture about testing to recovery hardness, not an unconditional exclusion of polynomial-time algorithms. Its model and hypothesis restrictions matter when applying it to a particular choice of a,b.

The precise conjecture in that paper also matters. Its bounded test functions must have expectation bounded below under the planted distribution. The authors explain that a broader earlier version was refuted using rare events. Thus citing a generic “low-degree conjecture” without stating that a hypothesis remains unproved would erase both the conditional nature of the result and an actual correction in the underlying evidence.

A 2026 revision of work by Chin, Mossel, Sohn and Wein gives efficient recovery below the usual boundary when the number of communities grows sufficiently quickly, in particular in a regime above √n. This is an important warning against treating the threshold as universal over every block model. Here q is fixed before n tends to infinity. Even a very large fixed q eventually lies below √n, so the growing-community algorithm does not supply the fixed-parameter example requested.

Settling this problem would test whether a threshold suggested by local propagation describes all efficient global algorithms in a basic random graph model. A new algorithm would identify exploitable structure missed by the familiar threshold calculation. A rigorous barrier would give a particularly clean example in which unlimited inference and efficient inference have different capabilities, with the data distribution specified by only three constants.
why: Determine whether the canonical local signal threshold is a true barrier for every efficient algorithm in a basic model of network inference.

importance.reason: A central, sharply parameterized computational-versus-statistical gap linking sparse random graphs, inference, message passing and average-case complexity.

progress.text: Abbe–Sandon prove efficient recovery above the Kesten–Stigum threshold for all fixed community counts; preprint 2015, revised 2016, journal publication 2018.
Banks–Moore–Neeman–Netrapalli prove information-theoretic recovery below the threshold in suitable assortative regimes with q≥11, using a potentially exponential algorithm.
Ding–Hua–Slot–Steurer’s revised paper derives recovery lower bounds under its explicitly restricted low-degree conjecture; Theorem A.1 allows a fixed gap below the threshold.

Chin–Mossel–Sohn–Wein revise their many-community analysis, correcting the proof of Theorem 1.2. Their below-threshold algorithms require a growing community count and do not settle the fixed-q question.

status_note: Efficient recovery above the threshold and information-theoretic recovery below it in suitable fixed-q assortative regimes are proved. The checked fixed-community computational lower bound remains conditional on an unproved low-degree conjecture. Growing-community algorithms in the August 2026 revision concern a different quantifier regime. No unconditional settlement of this precise fixed-q question found through 11 September 2026.
